question: Using only the text of the original 1787 Constitution: which federal offices does it set a minimum age for? For each, give the minimum age, the required years of citizenship or residence, and any other personal qualification the text states for that office.
reference: Three offices. A Representative (Article I, Section 2) must be at least 25 years old, a citizen of the United States for seven years, and, when elected, an inhabitant of the State in which he is chosen. A Senator (Article I, Section 3) must be at least 30, a citizen for nine years, and, when elected, an inhabitant of the State for which he is chosen. The President (Article II, Section 1) must be a natural born citizen (or a citizen at the time the Constitution was adopted), at least 35 years old, and fourteen years a resident within the United States. The original text sets no separate age for the Vice President.

Article II, Section 1: the Vice President is chosen for the same four-year term as the President; after the President is chosen, the person with the greatest number of electoral votes becomes Vice President, and if two or more remain with equal votes the Senate chooses the Vice President from them by ballot; if the President is removed, dies, resigns or cannot discharge the office, its powers and duties devolve on the Vice President, and Congress may by law declare which officer acts as President when both the President and the Vice President are gone. question: The agent-architectures survey presents five single-agent methods. Name them and, for each one, give the limitations the survey says it has.
reference: ReAct, RAISE, Reflexion, AutoGPT+P and LATS (Section 3). ReAct: the model can repetitively generate the same thoughts and actions and fail to create new thoughts that finish the task and exit the ReAct loop (human feedback would help). RAISE: it struggles to understand complex logic, and its agents often hallucinate about their roles or knowledge (a sales agent may start writing Python code); fine-tuning helped, but hallucination remains a limitation. Reflexion: it is susceptible to non-optimal local minima solutions, and it keeps long-term memory in a sliding window rather than a database, so memory is limited by the model's token limit; it still has room to improve on tasks that need much diversity, exploration and reasoning. AutoGPT+P: tool selection accuracy varies (tools called inappropriately or stuck in loops), exploration can be illogical (looking for objects in the wrong place), and human interaction is limited (the agent cannot seek clarification and the user cannot modify or terminate the plan during execution). LATS: it uses more computational resources and takes more time than other single-agent methods, and it was tested only on relatively simple question answering benchmarks, not on scenarios with tool calling or complex reasoning.

question: Both the BGE-M3 paper and the best-practices RAG paper use Faiss, Lucene and Pyserini. For each paper, say what each of the three is used for. Which vector database does the best-practices paper pick for its final system instead, and why?
reference: BGE-M3: on MIRACL it follows the official benchmark and evaluates with Pyserini; the Dense method builds a dense index with Faiss to search the top-1000 candidates, and the Sparse method builds a sparse index with Lucene for its top-1000; in Appendix C.2 the Lucene Analyzer is used as BM25's tokenizer and beats BM25 with the XLM-RoBERTa tokenizer (MIRACL 38.5 vs 31.9, MKQA 40.9 vs 39.9, MLDR 64.1 vs 53.6). Best practices: the BM25 and Contriever baselines use Pyserini's default implementations, and the retrieval experiments and evaluation are run with the Pyserini toolkit; the BM25 index is built with Lucene on the MS MARCO collections and the dense vector index with Faiss in a Flat configuration (Appendix A.2). Faiss is also one of five vector databases compared in Table 5 (with Weaviate, Chroma, Qdrant and Milvus); it has multiple index types but no billion-scale support, hybrid search or cloud-native features. The paper picks Milvus, the only one meeting all four criteria (multiple index types, billion-scale vectors, hybrid search, cloud-native), and builds its vector database in Milvus with 10 million English Wikipedia texts and 4 million medical texts.
